turns.text: What’s the very first thing you remember about arriving in Beidahuang from Shanghai? What did it look, smell, or sound like when you stepped off the train?

The air felt like it wanted to cut through my coat. I remember stepping from the train and seeing nothing familiar—just a flatness that went on and on, fields covered in a crust of old snow and mud. The wind was sharp, carrying the smell of wet earth and coal smoke from a distant stove. My shoes sank into the slush as soon as I stepped down; the mud sucked at my heels. I could hear the low voices of others who had arrived with me, but mostly it was the wind, always the wind, louder than anything I’d known in Shanghai. No city noise, no traffic, just emptiness and the feeling that the world had grown much larger and colder all at once.

Your description makes me feel how exposed and out of place you must have felt, especially with the wind and emptiness after coming from a busy city. You mentioned the smell of coal smoke from a distant stove—do you remember where you spent your first night there, and what it was like trying to sleep in that new place?

We were led to a low, drafty building that looked like it might have been a storage shed once. Inside, the walls were rough and bare, and the only warmth came from a single iron stove in the corner. I remember huddling with the others on a wooden platform, wrapped in all the clothes I had, using my bag as a pillow. The floor was hard and smelled faintly of damp straw. I could hear the wind rattling the windows and someone coughing nearby. I lay awake a long time, listening to those unfamiliar sounds and feeling every ache in my body from the train ride. I kept thinking about my bed at home—how soft it was, the weight of the blanket, the hum of traffic outside. Here, even sleep felt like something I had to fight for.

I can almost picture that—the rough wood, the cold that doesn’t let you rest, the way the absence of city sounds makes everything feel sharper. When you were lying awake that first night, did you feel more afraid or more angry? Or was it something else—maybe just numbness?

That first night, it was mostly a dull ache—like my mind wouldn’t let me feel anything too strongly yet. I remember turning my face to the wall and trying to picture home, but the images kept slipping away. I wasn’t angry, not yet, and fear felt too big to fit inside me. Mostly, I felt hollowed out, like I’d left something essential behind on the train. I listened to the others breathing and coughing, and I wondered if they felt as empty as I did, or if they were already braver than me.

It’s striking how you describe that emptiness, almost like a protective shell. You mentioned listening to the others breathing and coughing in the dark—did you eventually talk to any of them about how you were feeling, or did everyone keep those feelings to themselves at first?

Most of us kept quiet, especially in those first days. We moved around each other, sharing the same cramped space, but not the things that mattered. In the mornings, I’d see the tired faces, red eyes, and no one would say much beyond what was needed for the day’s work. Sometimes, while waiting for food or huddling near the stove, someone would let slip a sigh or a muttered complaint about the cold, but that was as far as it went. I remember once, after a long day in the fields, a girl next to me whispered that she couldn’t remember the sound of her mother’s voice anymore. She said it like she was talking to herself, not to anyone in particular. I didn’t answer. I was afraid that if I started talking about what I missed or how lost I felt, I might not be able to stop. So we all wore that shell, pretending it was just the weather that made us quiet.

That image of everyone pretending it was just the weather that made them quiet really stays with me. When you heard that girl whisper about forgetting her mother’s voice, did it change anything for you—did it make you feel less alone, or did it make the distance from home feel even sharper?

It made the distance sharper, like a sudden ache in the chest. Her words hung in the air for a moment, and I felt this jolt of recognition—she was feeling what I was, but saying it out loud made it real in a way I was trying to avoid. For a second, I wanted to reach out, maybe even say something back, but instead I turned away. After that, I found myself thinking about my own mother’s voice, trying to replay it in my head so I wouldn’t lose it too. It was comforting to know I wasn’t the only one, but it also made the whole place feel even more cut off and foreign, as if we were all drifting farther from home with every day of silence.

It sounds like hearing someone else’s pain out loud was almost dangerous, like it threatened to crack that protective shell you were all holding onto. Did you ever resent the people or the system that put you in that position—so far from home, forced into silence—or did you just focus on surviving each day?

Most days, I didn’t let myself think about blame—survival took up all the space in my head. But sometimes, usually when I was too tired to push the thoughts away, I’d feel this slow-burning resentment, not just at the people who made the decisions, but at the whole world that seemed to have turned upside down. It never felt safe to say those things out loud, so I’d swallow them and go back to counting the hours until I could sleep. The silence wasn’t just between us—it was inside me too, like a wall I had to keep patching up so I wouldn’t fall apart.

That image of patching up an inner wall so you wouldn’t fall apart is so vivid—it makes me think about how much energy it must have taken just to hold yourself together. Was there ever a moment, maybe something small or unexpected, that broke through that wall and made you feel human again, even for a little while?

One evening after a long day in the fields, I was washing mud from my hands at the pump when I heard someone humming a tune I recognized from the radio back home. It was quiet, almost lost in the sound of water splashing, but I knew it right away. My throat tightened. I didn’t say anything, but I found myself humming along under my breath. For a few minutes, I wasn’t just a body doing work—I was a girl from Shanghai who still remembered music, who still had a voice. The cold and the ache faded for a little while. Later, lying in the dark, I replayed that tune in my mind and let myself believe, just for a moment, that not everything had been taken from me.

The way music gave you back a piece of your old self, even if only for a moment, is really moving. Did you ever find other ways—maybe through writing, or something else—to hold onto your identity or memories from home, or was music the only escape?
